title: Position: Adopt Constraints Over Fixed Penalties in Deep Learning
claim: Finding a penalty coefficient that meets a target constraint level needs repeated trial-and-error search, since each trial is a full training run.
layout: single scatter plot, log-x, numbered points converging on a dotted target line
description: A single square scatter plot. The x-axis is the penalty coefficient c on a log scale, from 1e-3 to 1e0. The y-axis is achieved model density, from 0 to 1. A horizontal dotted gray line at 0.50 is labeled 'Target density'. Dark star markers carry numeric labels showing the bisection iterations. The two endpoints are both labeled 0: one at c=1e-3 with density about 0.85, and one at c=1 with density about 0.25. Iteration 1 sits at about 0.68 density, and iterations 2 to 5 zigzag in a tight cluster around c≈0.2–0.4, crossing the target line. The eye goes first to the dotted target line and then to the stars converging on it. The plot is grayscale with light gridlines.
caption: Solving a sparsity-constrained classification problem. Starting from coefficients yielding low (25%) and high (85%) model density, five bisection search steps are needed to reach the desired 50% density. \captioncomment{Numbers mark iterations (endpoints are "0"). Replicates Fig. 5(b) of [ref] (Appendix [ref]).}
abstract: Deep learning models are increasingly subject to explicit requirements, or constraints, such as safety levels, fairness limits, and sparsity budgets. In practice, such requirements are often handled through fixed weighted-sum penalization: the constraints are added to the task loss with fixed coefficients, and the resulting scalarized objective is minimized. This position paper argues that fixed penalization is often ill-suited to deep learning problems with non-negotiable requirements, for three main reasons. First, in non-convex settings, the penalized and constrained problems are not, in general, equivalent, so a minimizer of the penalized objective need not solve the constrained problem. Second, a penalty coefficient sets an objective-constraint trade-off rather than the constraint level, so finding an acceptable coefficient often takes trial and error, each trial a full training run. Third, fixed penalization weakens hard requirements into soft penalties to be traded off against task performance. As a result, compliance is no longer built into the problem, and requirements can be quietly relaxed. We therefore argue that, when a deep learning problem specifies non-negotiable requirements, one should solve the constrained problem itself instead of a surrogate defined by fixed penalization.
